title: Take It Back
objectives: I can use the prefixes dis-, mis-, and pre- to figure out what a word means.
I can split a word into a prefix and a base word.
I can use ten words with prefixes in my own sentences.
I can explain how a prefix changes the meaning of a base word.
rationale: After un- and re-, third graders are ready for three more prefixes that unlock many verbs and adjectives. Each word in this unit is a clear base word plus a prefix: dis- (not, opposite of), mis- (wrongly, badly), and pre- (before). Students learn to find the base, read the prefix, and combine the meanings, then check the result against the sentence. Several bases (honest, obey, trust, lead, treat, view) are words students already use, so the prefix is the only new piece. This is the second prefix unit of the year and sets up suffix work in units 17 and beyond.

words.def: Not telling the truth; likely to lie or cheat.
words.ex: The dishonest player moved her piece when no one was looking.
words.ex2: It is dishonest to say you finished your work when you did not.
words.nonExample: A person who returns a lost wallet is not dishonest.

apps.academic: In social studies, we discuss why a dishonest leader loses people's trust.
apps.spoken: Copying my friend's answer would be dishonest.
apps.writing: Use dishonest to show that a character lies or cheats.

cloze2.s: Hiding the broken lamp and blaming the cat was a ___ thing to do.

misuse.s: The dishonest girl was well known for always telling the truth and never cheating.
misuse.why: Dishonest means not truthful, so always telling the truth is the opposite.

words.def: To not do what a rule or a person in charge says.
words.ex: The puppy will disobey and run off when it sees a squirrel.
words.ex2: Players who disobey the rules may have to sit out of the game.
words.nonExample: Following the lifeguard's instructions is not disobeying.

apps.academic: In stories, a character who chooses to disobey may cause a problem.
apps.spoken: I would never disobey a safety rule.
apps.writing: Use disobey for choosing not to follow a rule or order.

cloze.s: The boy chose to ___ the sign that said no swimming, and the lifeguard called him out.

cloze2.s: If you ___ the traffic light and cross against it, you could be in danger.

misuse.s: She will disobey the rule by following every word of it exactly as it was written.
misuse.why: Disobey means not following a rule; following every word is the opposite.

words.frame: Someone who disobeys a rule might ___.

words.def: To separate things that were joined together.
words.ex: Please disconnect the cord from the wall before you clean the lamp.
words.ex2: The train workers had to disconnect the last car from the others.
words.nonExample: Snapping two toy blocks together is not disconnecting them.

apps.academic: In science, we disconnect a wire to stop the flow of electricity in a circuit.
apps.spoken: Disconnect the charger when the battery is full.
apps.writing: Use disconnect to say that two joined things are pulled apart.

cloze.s: Before changing the bulb, Dad told us to ___ the lamp from the wall socket.

cloze2.s: The conductor had to ___ the engine from the long line of train cars at the end of the route.

misuse.s: To disconnect the two puzzle pieces, she pushed them together until they snapped in tight.
misuse.why: Disconnect means to pull apart, so pushing together is the opposite.

visual.alt: A plug and a train car.

words.frame: I would disconnect the ___ from the ___.

words.def: To feel that you cannot believe or rely on someone.
words.ex: Many people distrust a salesperson who promises too much.
words.ex2: After the broken promise, Jada began to distrust her friend.
words.nonExample: Letting a close friend borrow your bike is not an act of distrust.

apps.academic: In history, people may distrust a leader who breaks promises.
apps.spoken: I distrust any website that asks for my password.
apps.writing: Use distrust for a feeling that someone or something cannot be relied on.

cloze.s: The cat began to ___ the vet after the shot, and it hid under the couch at every visit.

cloze2.s: Readers may ___ a story that has no facts, no sources, and no names.

misuse.s: She was ready to distrust her best friend, so she told her every secret right away.
misuse.why: Distrust means to feel you cannot rely on someone; sharing every secret shows the opposite.

words.def: To make someone believe something that is not true.
words.ex: A shadow on the wall can mislead you into thinking someone is in the room.
words.ex2: The wrong arrow on the sign misled the hikers, and they walked the wrong way.
words.nonExample: Giving a friend clear and correct directions does not mislead.

apps.academic: In science, a bad graph can mislead readers about the facts.
apps.spoken: Please do not mislead me; tell me what happened.
apps.writing: Use mislead when someone gives a wrong idea, on purpose or by mistake.

cloze.s: A sign pointing the wrong way can ___ travelers and send them far off course.

cloze2.s: The ad was ___ because it showed a giant burger, but the real one was tiny.

misuse.s: The guide misled the group by giving them the exact right map and a true story.
misuse.why: Mislead means to give a wrong idea; a right map and a true story do the opposite.

words.frame: A sign could mislead people if ___.

words.def: To be unkind or harmful to a person or animal.
words.ex: It is wrong to mistreat a pet by leaving it out in the cold.
words.ex2: The rules say visitors must not mistreat the museum displays.
words.nonExample: Giving a pet fresh water and gentle care is not mistreating it.

apps.academic: In social studies, we learn how laws protect people who were mistreated.
apps.spoken: No one should mistreat an animal.
apps.writing: Use mistreat when someone is cruel or careless toward a living thing or an object.

cloze.s: It is cruel to ___ an animal by never giving it food or a warm place to sleep.

cloze2.s: The librarian was upset to see someone ___ the old books by tearing out the pages.

misuse.s: The kind farmer would mistreat his horses by brushing them every day and giving them fresh hay.
misuse.why: Mistreat means to be unkind to; brushing and feeding is kind care.

words.def: To put something where you cannot find it again.
words.ex: Dad always seems to misplace his keys right before work.
words.ex2: I misplaced my glove, and we searched the whole classroom for it.
words.nonExample: Hanging your coat on its own hook is not misplacing it.

apps.academic: In school, a student may misplace a worksheet and need a new copy.
apps.spoken: I always misplace one sock from each pair.
apps.writing: Use misplace for putting something somewhere and forgetting where.

cloze.s: Lena tends to ___ her pencil case, and she checks every desk before she finds it.

cloze2.s: If you ___ your library book, tell the librarian right away so you can look for it together.

misuse.s: She misplaced her hat by keeping it on her head and knowing exactly where it was.
misuse.why: Misplace means to lose track of where something is; she knows where her hat is.

words.def: A look at something before everyone else sees it.
words.ex: We watched a preview of the new movie at the theater.
words.ex2: The teacher gave us a preview of next week's science lesson.
words.nonExample: Seeing a whole movie after it has been out for months is not a preview.

apps.academic: Before reading a chapter, take a preview of the headings and pictures.
apps.spoken: The preview made me want to read the book.
apps.writing: Use preview for a first look at something that comes later.

cloze.s: The class got a ___ of the play when the actors performed one short scene on Friday.

cloze2.s: Mom gave me a ___ of the surprise by showing one small picture of it.

misuse.s: The preview of the movie came out after the movie ended and everyone went home.
misuse.why: A preview comes before the real thing, not after it.

words.def: From a time long ago, before people kept written records.
words.ex: The museum has a prehistoric skeleton that is thousands of years old.
words.ex2: Prehistoric people used stone tools to hunt and build.
words.nonExample: A smartphone from last year is not prehistoric.

apps.academic: In science, fossils help us learn about prehistoric plants and animals.
apps.spoken: Some cave paintings are prehistoric art.
apps.writing: Use prehistoric for a time before writing was used.

cloze.s: Scientists dug up a ___ bone that was far older than any book or map.

cloze2.s: The ___ cave paintings showed hunters and animals from a time before there were any letters.

misuse.s: The prehistoric robot was built last week and has a bright, brand-new screen.
misuse.why: Prehistoric means from before written records, not from last week.

words.def: To warm an oven or pan before you put food in it.
words.ex: Please preheat the oven so the muffins bake evenly.
words.ex2: Chef Ana preheated the pan before she cracked the eggs into it.
words.nonExample: Turning on the oven only after the cookies are inside is not preheating.

apps.academic: In a science recipe, we preheat the oven so the temperature is steady.
apps.spoken: I always preheat the oven before baking.
apps.writing: Use preheat to tell what happens before cooking starts.

cloze.s: Mom turned on the oven early to ___ it, so it would be hot when the pizza was ready to go in.

cloze2.s: Always ___ the pan before you add the batter, so the pancakes cook evenly.

misuse.s: To preheat the oven, put the cold cake in first and then turn the oven on.
misuse.why: Preheat means to warm the oven before the food goes in.

passage.title: A Museum Saturday
paras: On Saturday, Jin and her cousin Leo visited the science museum. A guide gave them a short preview of the new prehistoric exhibit. "Stay on the path," she said. "A sign asks visitors not to mistreat the displays by touching or leaning on them." Leo wanted to disobey, but Jin gave him a look, and he put his hands in his pockets.

In the dinosaur hall, Leo saw two signs about one fossil. Each sign gave a different age. "One of these signs must mislead visitors," he said. "I distrust them both." Jin laughed. "Let's ask the guide." The guide explained that one sign was old and had not been fixed. It was not dishonest, only out of date.

Later, at home, Jin's mom asked her to preheat the oven for muffins. Jin could not find the recipe card. "I must have misplaced it," she said. She found it under a pile of mail. Before she began mixing, she had to disconnect the mixer from the wall to change its blades.
The muffins smelled wonderful. Leo said it was the best end to a day of learning.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "mislead" most nearly means
qs.why: Leo thinks one sign is wrong, so he says it might give visitors a wrong idea.

qs.q: Why does Jin give Leo a look in paragraph 1?
choices: She wants him to touch the bones.
She is bored with the tour.
She wants him to follow the guide's rule.
qs.why: The guide told them not to touch the displays, so Jin wants Leo to follow the rule.

qs.q: Which detail shows the old sign was not dishonest?
choices: The guide said the sign was old and not fixed yet.
Leo said he distrusted both signs.
The signs were in the dinosaur hall.
qs.why: The guide explains the sign was simply out of date, not a lie.

qs.q: What is a central idea of the passage?
choices: Jin and Leo spent a day learning and used careful thinking about what they read.
qs.why: The story shows them learning at the museum and thinking about the signs.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words built from the prefixes dis-, mis-, and pre-, read a short story that uses all ten, and practice splitting words into prefix and base to find the meaning.

notes.va.dishonest.adj: Model the split: dis + honest. Ask: what is the opposite of honest? Students may say lying, which is a start.
notes.va.disobey.v: Dis + obey. Link to obedient from the earlier unit. Ask for examples of a rule and what disobeying it could cause.
notes.va.disconnect.v: Dis + connect. Use two connected blocks and pull them apart. Students may only know it for the internet; widen to plugs and train cars.
notes.va.distrust.v: Dis + trust. Distrust is not hate; it is not being able to rely on someone. Practice with a mild example.
notes.va.mislead.v: Mis + lead. The past form is misled; teach it. Mislead can happen on purpose or by mistake, as with a wrong sign.
notes.va.mistreat.v: Mis + treat. Handle gently with students: use examples with objects and pets, such as tearing a library book.
notes.va.misplace.v: Mis + place. It means to lose track of where something is. Ask students to share a time they misplaced something and found it.
notes.va.preview.n: Pre + view. Use a movie trailer and a book's headings as examples. Ask: when does a preview happen, before or after?
notes.va.prehistoric.adj: Pre + historic. Prehistoric means before people wrote records. Tie to dinosaurs, but note that dinosaurs lived far earlier than early people.
notes.va.preheat.v: Pre + heat. Compare with heat. Say: preheat happens before the food goes in.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: "I see disconnect. I can split it: dis- means not or the opposite of, and connect means to join. So disconnect means to undo a join. In the sentence, Jin unplugs the mixer from the wall, so the meaning fits."
discuss: Which prefix helps you the most when you read a new word?
How can you tell if a word starts with a prefix or just starts with those letters, like discover or mister?
misconceptions: Any word that starts with dis- means not.
Mis- always means a mistake was made by accident.
Preview is the same as review.
extend: Make a poster of one prefix with five real words.
Look in a favorite book for words that start with dis-, mis-, or pre- and decide whether each has a prefix and base.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit the three prefixes after two days with a quick sort of word cards, and again at one week with new words. Pair disobey with obedient, and distrust with courteous and unlikely when discussing character behavior.

wida.oral: Partner A says a base word; Partner B adds dis-, mis-, or pre- if it makes a real word and tells what the new word means.
